 BACK WHEN: Armistice Day big in Port Angeles
 Published 1:30 am Saturday, November 7, 2026
 By John McNutt For Peninsula Daily News 
 1/2 
 Swipe or click to see more 
 2/2 
 Swipe or click to see more 
 Getting your Trinity Audio player ready... 
 ON NOV. 11, WE will celebrate Veterans Day. It is the day when we honor military veterans of the United States. And well we should.
 So many people have died in service to our nation. So many have been severely injured in service to our nation. So many have been at the ready. Veterans Day is a holiday dedicated to American veterans of all wars.
 Like so many holidays, the focus has evolved over time.
 The origins of Veterans Day began with Armistice Day in 1918. A temporary cessation of hostilities between the Allied forces and Germany was set at the 11th hour of the 11th day of the 11th month. The Treaty of Versailles was finally signed on June 28, 1919.
 In November 1919, President Woodrow Wilson proclaimed Nov. 11 as the first commemoration of Armistice Day.
 On Nov. 11, 1921, an unidentified American soldier killed during World War I was buried at Arlington National Cemetery. Every Veterans Day recognizes the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier, which now includes unknowns from World War II, Korea and Vietnam.
 Armistice Day did recognize the sacrifices made by American soldiers. But it also had another purpose. On June 4, 1926, Congress passed a resolution that the “recurring anniversary of Nov. 11, 1918, should be commemorated with thanksgiving and exercises designated to perpetuate peace through good will and mutual understanding between nations.”
 So how was Armistice Day celebrated in Port Angeles in 1926?
 In 1926 the tragedies of World War I were still fresh in many people’s minds. Many of our own friends, family, and neighbors fought in that war.
 It started on Sunday, Nov. 7, 1926, with an Armistice Day service at the Lincoln Memorial Congregational Church. The service was led by the Rev. Stuart Goude, who was also the Chaplain of the Walter Akeley Post of the American Legion.
 The morning Armistice Day service included a sermon using the text “Peace on Earth.” His sermon was meant to remember those who sacrificed for peace while reflecting on the biblical vision of harmony and reconciliation. Goude encouraged people to pursue peace.
 The evening service was unusual and followed the theme of “The Message of the Bugle.” With Goude, there were four veterans on the platform; Sgt. Lazlo represented the local American Legion post and was the bugler. The other three veterans were Ed Schlager, commander of the American Legion, representing the American soldiers; Dr. Hamilton, representing the Canadian forces; and W. R. Gibson, representing the English forces.
 Goude’s message centered on the bugle calls used by the armed forces. Bugler Lazlo sounded First Call, Reveille, Church Call, Fatigue Call, Drill Call, Retreat, and Star-Spangled Banner.
 With each bugle call, Goude gave an “explanation for those who had not been in the service, and also gave apt quotations which caused the calls to come with a real message for all.”
 The service ended with Taps being played. Goude pointed out that, “Though the other calls may stir in our hearts the military spirit and a feeling of the so-called glory of war, the plaintive, a strangely beautiful call of Taps brings us back to the realization that war is not glorious. War is death.”
 On the following Tuesday, Nov. 9, Mayor Hedrick issued a proclamation:
 “Whereas, the national and state governments have seen fit to set aside November 11 as a day of remembrance of that morning when news of an armistice came like a ray of sunshine along the western front, and
 “Whereas, the American Legion boys of Port Angeles are serving well in time of peace as they did in the time of war,
 “Therefore, the mayor of your city believes that the least we can do is to close our places of business and meditate just a bit on the wars of the past and be thankful for the peace that permits us to enjoy freedom to the fullest.”
 Local businesses, banks, and government offices were closed on Nov. 11.
 The local schools were given a half-holiday. They started at 8 a.m. and ended their day at noon. Members of the American Legion spoke at the local schools.
 Many high school students took advantage of the early dismissal to travel to Port Townsend for the “big game.” The “big game” was an Armistice Day football game at Port Townsend. Many local businessmen attended the “big game” Port Angeles lost 9 to 6 on a late-game drop-kick field goal.
 The day ended with two events. First, a banquet for all veterans was prepared. It was not limited to members of the American Legion. Rather, it was open to all who served with the Allies during World War I. The banquet began at 6:30 p.m. and the veterans were served by members of the Women’s Relief Corps.
 The evening ended with the Second Annual Armistice Day Ball sponsored by the American Legion and hosted at the Masonic Temple. A highlight of the ball included playing some of the songs the soldiers used to sing while they were “over there.”
 Howard Savage, National Commander of the American Legion stated, “Armistice Day is the service man’s day. It is a day which should be made sacred to the memory of those brave men who went over to Flanders Field, but never returned.” Savage also stated, “God knows, we do not want another war. We should be ever at peace, but ever prepared.”
 Peace and neutrality were strong public sentiments in the United States due to the horrors if World War I. Public sentiment changed when Pearl Harbor was attacked.
 During the 1927 legislative session, Washington declared Nov. 11 as a holiday. In 1938, Armistice Day (Nov. 11) became a federal holiday. In 1954, the name was changed to Veterans Day.
 It is important to remember the historical context of Armistice Day, which is now Veterans Day. It is important and significant for us to remember all those who sacrificed for our peace. At the same time, we should heed the call to pursue peace so our children will not have to make the ultimate sacrifice.

 John McNutt is a descendant of Clallam County pioneers and treasurer of the North Olympic History Center Board of Directors. He can be reached at woodrowsilly@gmail.com .
